sentences.text: The broad-billed parrot possessed a disproportionately large head and jaws, featuring a skull that was flattened from top to bottom.
Ridges on the skull indicate it had a distinct frontal crest of feathers that was firmly attached and could not be raised or lowered.
Research suggests the head was blue, with a beak that may have been red and greyish or blackish plumage.
The broad-billed parrot likely vanished from the world around the 1680s, though the IUCN status system lists the extinction year as 1693.
The first illustration of the parrot appeared alongside the first drawing of a dodo in reports published in 1601.
Dutch ships' journals from 1598 onwards first referred to the bird as the "Indian raven".
The broad-billed parrot likely ate hard seeds from various Mauritian plants such as Latania loddigesii, Mimusops maxima, Sideroxylon grandiflorum, Diospyros egrettorium, and Pandanus utilis.
In 2020, Joanna K. Carpenter and colleagues suggested the broad-billed parrot was an important seed disperser capable of destroying large seeds found low in the Mascarene flora.
However, Holyoak argued based on radiographs that the broad-billed parrot had a weakly constructed mandible and likely fed on soft fruits instead of hard seeds.
Analysis of the underlying pencil sketch suggests the wings were not particularly short but appeared broad like forest-adapted species, with a large alula characteristic of slow-flying birds.
Historical accounts state the bird could fly with difficulty, and illustrations show it perched on trees, which is improbable for a flightless bird.
Hume stated in 2007 that the broad-billed parrot's poor flight, large size, and tameness made it easy prey for sailors and vulnerable to introduced crab-eating macaques and rats.
The broad-billed parrot is classified as a member of the tribe Psittaculini.
The taxonomic affinities of the broad-billed parrot remain undetermined.
The broad-billed parrot was endemic to the island of Mauritius in the Mascarene Islands.
The genus Lophopsittacus lived during the Holocene, from 0.0117 to 0 million years ago.
The broad-billed parrot is believed to have gone extinct by the 1680s due to large-scale harvesting of its palm food sources.
Emile Oustalet argued in 1897 and France Staub as late as 1993 that the "Indian raven" was a hornbill, though no hornbill remains have been found on the island.
Many authors, including the Newton brothers, inferred the bird was flightless based on the apparent short wings and large size in the 1601 sketch, though this is debated.
